analysis.one_liner: Moves most large class action lawsuits from state to federal courts and restricts attorney fees in coupon settlements.
analysis.headline: A procedural vote to cut off Senate debate failed 44-43 on July 8, 2004 — far short of the 60 needed — so the bill never got an up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten where big class action lawsuits can be heard. Most class actions over $5 million involving parties from different states would move from state courts, where consumer groups say plaintiffs historically fare better, into federal courts, where the standards for forming a class are harder to meet [S3]. The bill also adds rules aimed at abusive settlements — limits on attorney fees when class members get only coupons, and protections against settlements that pay some class members less just for living far from the courthouse [S2] [S3]. Critics argued those consumer protections were window dressing around the bill's main effect: making it much harder for consumers with small-dollar claims against banks, insurers, and manufacturers to sue as a group.
analysis.who_benefits: Large corporations facing consumer class actions — banks, insurers, product makers, and other consumer-facing businesses — gain the most, because cases would shift to federal courts where class actions are harder to certify and where the bill's removal provisions let any single defendant pull a case out of state court [S3]. Class members stuck with coupon settlements and low-value awards would nominally benefit from the new fee and settlement rules [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large corporate defendants in class actions

how_it_helps.text: Federal courts would get jurisdiction over interstate class actions exceeding $5 million, and any defendant could remove such a case from state court without the consent of all defendants [S3].

Attorney fees in coupon settlements would be based on the actual value of coupons class members redeem, and courts would have to find a settlement fair, reasonable, and adequate before approving coupon awards [S2] [S3].

The bill bars settlements that pay class members less solely because they live farther from the court, and requires notice of proposed settlements to federal and state officials, including bank regulators for depository-institution defendants [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers with small-dollar claims bear the cost. Many consumer fraud and product claims are worth only a few dollars per person and only work as class actions; shifting them to federal court, where courts read class certification requirements more strictly, would make many of those cases impossible to bring. State courts would also lose settlements and fee awards that currently flow through them.

drawbacks.text: Abusive coupon settlements are a real problem — class counsel can win multimillion-dollar fees while class members get coupons worth little — and this bill directly targets that by valuing fees on redeemed coupons and requiring written fairness findings [S2] [S3].

The bill's findings state that class members often get little or nothing from class actions, notices are confusing, and state courts sometimes act with bias against out-of-state defendants — problems a federal forum is meant to address [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the jurisdiction change, not the fee rules, is the bill's engine: moving cases to federal court makes them harder to certify, which reduces recoveries for consumers even in cases with no settlement abuse.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The settlement-abuse provisions are genuine but narrow; the bill's main work is the jurisdictional shift, which benefits corporate defendants far more than it benefits class members. The carve-out for securities claims [S3] also shows the rules were designed selectively. The costs to consumers' ability to band together outweigh the protections the bill offers them.

outcome.mechanism: Republican leaders brought the bill to the Senate floor in July 2004, but the vote to cut off debate got only 44 of the 60 senators needed, so it never came to an up-or-down vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2004 by Senator Grassley with 11 original cosponsors and placed directly on the Senate calendar [S1] [S5].
In May 2004, a motion to proceed to the bill and its cloture motion were both withdrawn, an early sign of trouble finding the votes [S5].

On July 6-8, 2004, the Senate took the bill up by unanimous consent, and Senator Frist moved to recommit it to the Judiciary Committee with instructions to report back immediately with an amendment (SA 3550) [S5].
Cloture failed on July 8, 2004, by a vote of 44-43 — 16 votes short of the 60 needed to end debate and reach a final vote [S6].
The vote split sharply by party: 42 of 51 Republicans voted to cut off debate while only 2 of 48 Democrats did; the one Independent voted no [S6].
The bill received no further action before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, consumers kept full access to state courts for class actions, and corporate defendants did not get the easier federal forum or removal rights they sought. Plaintiff-side class action firms and the state-court system also kept the status quo, while the settlement-abuse provisions that would have capped coupon-settlement fees never took effect either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers kept state-court access; defendants lost

sides.party_line_note: On the decisive cloture vote, 42 of 51 Republicans voted yes while only 2 of 48 Democrats did, despite the bill's bipartisan roster of 13 cosponsors (6 Democrats, 7 Republicans) [S4] [S6].

industries.note: The bill gives special notice and regulator-involvement procedures for class actions against depository institutions and foreign banks, and the jurisdictional shift would move consumer suits against banks into federal court [S3]. Banks' interest in fewer and harder-to-bring consumer class actions runs against consumers seeking redress.

The bill carves out claims involving covered securities and corporate governance from its reach entirely, leaving the securities litigation system untouched while other industries lose their state-court advantages [S3].

industries.industry: Insurance, product manufacturers, and other consumer-facing corporate defendants
industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to let any defendant remove interstate class actions to federal court and to bar state courts from handling nationwide class actions, sharply reducing exposure to consumer class suits [S3].

The bill caps fees in coupon settlements at the redeemed value of coupons and pushes large cases into federal court, cutting both fee levels and case volume; this industry's fortunes largely rise and fall with consumers' ability to sue as a class [S3].
